lesson.title: Arccsc: The Absolute Value Strikes Again
lesson.summary: The derivative of arccsc x mirrors the arcsec derivation almost exactly, producing the negative counterpart -1/(|x| sqrt(x^2-1)).
lesson.body:
Cosecant has the same one to one problem secant did: csc y is undefined at y = 0. Restricting cosecant to the two piece domain [-pi/2, 0) union (0, pi/2] makes it one to one, covering every value with |x| >= 1, and arccsc x is defined for exactly those x.

Differentiating implicitly from csc y = x gives -csc y cot y times y' = 1, so y' = -1/(x cot y). From cot^2 y = csc^2 y - 1 = x^2 - 1, cot y = plus or minus sqrt(x^2-1), again depending on which piece y sits in. On (0, pi/2], x = csc y >= 1 and cot y >= 0, so cot y = sqrt(x^2-1), giving y' = -1/(x sqrt(x^2-1)), negative, matching x > 0. On [-pi/2, 0), x = csc y <= -1, and here sin y < 0 while cos y > 0, so cot y < 0, meaning cot y = -sqrt(x^2-1). Substituting gives y' = -1/(x times -sqrt(x^2-1)) = 1/(x sqrt(x^2-1)), and since x is negative on this piece, this equals -1/(|x| sqrt(x^2-1)) once rewritten with |x|. Both pieces unify into d/dx[arccsc x] = -1/(|x| sqrt(x^2-1)), always negative, matching the fact that arccsc decreases on each piece of its domain.

For practice, differentiate y = arccsc(5x), defined where |5x| >= 1, meaning |x| >= 1/5. With u = 5x and u' = 5, the chain rule gives dy/dx = -u'/(|u| sqrt(u^2-1)) = -5/(|5x| sqrt(25x^2-1)) = -5/(5|x| sqrt(25x^2-1)) = -1/(|x| sqrt(25x^2-1)). At x = 1, this gives -1/sqrt(24), negative as expected.

Secant and cosecant are reciprocal cofunctions of each other, and their inverse derivatives differ only by a sign, the same clean relationship seen between arcsin and arccos two chapters back. Recognizing that pattern, rather than memorizing five unrelated formulas, is the real payoff of working through all five derivations in order.
